tier_reason: The README 'Modern Systems Languages' table (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, Arch Linux, 2026-09 sample run) has Hare 150=150+0.05 us/f against C gcc-15 392, gcc 16.2.1 454, g++-15 303, g++ 16.2.1 486, clang++ 236 and clang C 118, exactly as claimed; the harness code is public (cbench, MIT: bm_Hare, bm_C_and_Cxx_using_gcc, bm_C_and_Cxx_using_clang, gcc_clang_op_flags), compiler versions are in the table, flags are in the script and the CPU model is stated, so A holds.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Harness file cbench (the README's ./benchmark). Hare: 'hare build -o <bin>' in default (non-release) mode, HARECACHE pointed at a fresh directory once per operation; the 'check' operation also runs 'hare build -o <tmp>', so Hare's Check column (135.9 us/f) is a full build. C with gcc and clang: '-Wall -Wextra' (clang also '-fno-color-diagnostics -fno-caret-diagnostics -fno-diagnostics-show-option'), no -O flag (GCC and Clang default -O0), build = compile plus link with '-o <bin>'. C++ with g++ and clang++: only '-Wno-c++11-extensions', no -O flag. Hare's QBE backend has no optimization levels and runs its fixed pass pipeline on every build. Linker and assembler versions are not stated.
corrections.caveats: repo_url is the canonical upstream named by packagers; git.sr.ht does not resolve from this sandbox (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the licence, star count and last commit of Hare itself are unverified (the GPL-3.0-only compiler and MPL-2.0 standard library split comes from packager metadata in search results). This is a compile-throughput claim for the toolchain (harec plus QBE against GCC's middle and back end), not a runtime or language-level win: clang compiling the same C file is faster than Hare (118 against 150 Total), so 'Hare faster than C' holds only against GCC and g++ and against clang++. The C/C++ side builds at -O0, which is GCC's fastest compile mode and so favours the baseline rather than crippling it, while QBE always runs its optimization passes. The workload is one synthetic 40000-function translation unit of i64 add chains with no headers and almost no standard library, so it does not predict real build times (the README says so). Within one invocation every repetition compiles byte-identical source (the constant pool and its index restart per file), and HARECACHE is wiped once per operation rather than per repetition, so the minimum-of-runs Hare build reuses standard-library modules (os, rt) cached by the first repetition, comparable to C linking a prebuilt libc; the 6-second per-build time shows the main module itself was not a cache hit. Tasks for all compilers run in parallel, one pinned worker per performance core, so concurrent builds share caches and memory bandwidth. The table is one sample run; the README's own Conclusions quote different numbers for the same machine (clang 87 us/f against 118 in the table, gcc 418 to 455 against 392 to 454), so results move by up to about 30% between samples, which does not threaten the 2.6x to 3.0x lead over GCC but does narrow the 1.6x lead over clang++. Warning flags are applied to C builds and not to Hare. The README was last edited 2026-10-12 (wording only) and its tables 2026-10-09.

notes: Numbers and harness verified in cbench and the README; A stands, but the win is the Hare toolchain against GCC and g++ (clang C is faster), so record it as compile throughput rather than a language-level runtime claim. why_faster from the source: the README attributes nothing to Hare; the plausible mechanism is QBE's small backend against GCC's GIMPLE/RTL pipeline, which runs even at -O0 (inference). Hare upstream metadata stays unverified because sr.ht is unreachable.

tier_reason: The committed results JSON files (results/2026-08-12, 2026-09-16, 2026-09-17) match every claimed number, but the suite is run by VictoriaMetrics, which sells VictoriaLogs, and no hardware is stated anywhere (info.json holds only the git hash), so first-party tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: results/2026-09-17 (vlagent v1.52.0 vs Fluent Bit v5.0.9): resources case average CPU 0.0476 vs 0.2040 cores (4.3x less, derived from page data), average memory 33152688 vs 56061519 bytes (1.7x less, derived from page data), max memory 46620672 vs 110538752 bytes, lost 0 vs 3; throughput case 177949 vs 41222 logs/s (4.3x, derived from page data), where the Fluent Bit run is marked Success false, FailReason OOMKilled, Lost 1133131, and the two collectors used 0.475 and 0.407 average cores, so neither reached its 1-CPU limit. The 2026-08-12 run (vlagent v1.48.0, Fluent Bit v4.2.3) gives 178274 vs 40218 logs/s and CPU 0.0479 vs 0.2116 cores; the 2026-09-16 run (same versions as 2026-08-12) gives 176712 vs 39734 logs/s and CPU 0.0478 vs 0.2131 cores.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark: VictoriaMetrics runs the suite and sells VictoriaLogs, so the tier is capped at C. Hardware is not stated (results/<date>/info.json records only the git hash, bd89fd0 for 2026-09-17). The Fluent Bit throughput run failed in all three committed rounds (OOMKilled, 252175 to 1133131 lines lost) while using about 0.41 to 0.43 cores, so the 41222 logs/s figure is a memory failure point caused by a missing Mem_Buf_Limit, not a CPU-bound capacity figure; the maintainers added Mem_Buf_Limit 512MB on 2026-09-23 (commit c53524a, 'Prevent FluentBit from OOMs') after these results were produced at bd89fd0, and no post-fix results are committed, so the throughput ratio rests on a crippled baseline and only the resources-case CPU and memory figures are a like-for-like comparison. vlagent itself peaked at 0.475 cores in the throughput case, so its 178k logs/s ceiling may be set by the generator or verifier rather than by vlagent. This is an application-against-application comparison of two different pipelines (Fluent Bit's tail input with kubernetes filter Merge_Log, vlagent's jsonline output with includeNodeLabels), not the same algorithm and not a Go-against-C language claim. Fluent Bit uses an untuned configuration close to the Helm chart defaults, and the README invites tuning PRs. Each collector is limited to 1 CPU and 1 GiB. The 2026-09-16 and 2026-09-17 rounds were committed together (commit 31266d0) to confirm node configuration did not change results. The published results page and blog post are on blocked hosts, so numbers here come from the committed JSON files only. One run per round per case.

notes: All numbers match the committed JSON; keep at C with the throughput case flagged as a crippled (OOM-killed, later-fixed config) baseline and the resources case (4.3x less CPU, 1.7x less memory at about 10k logs/s) as the usable claim. Not a language-level win: two different products and pipelines. why_faster stays unexplained by the source beyond the 20% native-format note in values/vlagent.yml.

tier_reason: The readme only says 'Very fast, high performance rasterizer with SIMD support' and 'Best performance is with LDC'; there is no benchmark directory, no numbers and no named baseline, and issue #8 discusses glyph speed against GDI without timings, so tier D.

corrections.caveats: No numbers and no baseline anywhere I could open, so this is a tier D record kept for the 'research' list. The orchestrator's lead (about 2x Cairo) does not appear in the readme, the issues or search results; issue #8 ('Test render speed of 1 glyph', closed 2021-06-29) compares against GDI with no timings, and the maintainer only estimates that a 4x glyph speedup is achievable through caching and pre-flattening, plus about 2x more from a planned font rasterizer. The dub registry page shows the same self-description (search snippet only). Single-threaded, 32 bpp only, 16-byte-aligned scanlines, x86 SSE2 required, work-in-progress API. Last commit 2022-05-06 (more than four years ago), 21 stars, not notable by the tier D rule. The category fits wave 10's rasterizers-2d better than systems-and-safety.

notes: Confirmed as tier D with no measurement and no baseline; keep-and-document rather than reject (low notability, abandoned, 21 stars). No language-level claim can be drawn: nothing compares the D code against Cairo or Blend2D.
